https://hungarytoday.hu/watermelon-growe.text: Watermelon Growers Hope Warmer Weather Revives Slumping Market This year’s season did not get off to a good start , and watermelon growers are expecting sales to pick up in the coming days, based on a market summary published Monday on the website of FruitVeB, the Hungarian Fruit and Vegetable Interprofessional Organization and Marketing Board. The organization attributed the unfavorable trends to the weather; the heat wave at the end of June accelerated ripening, resulting in an abundant supply by the first week of July, but demand fell as temperatures dropped. Photo: Pexels Based on the report, the two factors are closely linked: watermelon consumption is highest during heat waves and drops significantly in cooler weather. Although industry associations asked retail chains not to slash prices, by mid-month the chains were already advertising sales at prices around 150 forints per kilogram (0.41 euros per kilogram; 1 euro = 366 forints). While this is favorable for consumers, at this price level, producers do not earn enough revenue to cover their expenses. With intensive production methods, production costs reach 4–6 million forints per hectare (10,930–16,390 euros per hectare); therefore, an acceptable profit can only be expected if net producer prices average 100–120 forints per kilogram over the entire season, FruitVeB said. According to the report, by mid-July the European watermelon market had collapsed due to the weather, causing export prices to plummet; by the last third of the month, buyers were only willing to pay a net price of 40–50 forints per kilogram. Even so, part of the crop remained unsellable because producers in other countries were also trying to offload their inventories. Hungarian growers are now hoping that the warmer weather expected in the coming days will boost demand, and that import pressure will also ease, as the melon season in the Balkan countries is drawing to a close. In the first half of August, watermelons from Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg and Heves counties in eastern and northern Hungary will come onto the market in increasing quantities, but due to uncertainties, price trends are unpredictable. If consumption does not pick up, watermelon production in Hungary could decline next year. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Bashar al-Assad (pictured) and his brother Maher, who was also sentenced to death, fled to Moscow in December 2024. Photograph: ATPImages/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Bashar al-Assad (pictured) and his brother Maher, who was also sentenced to death, fled to Moscow in December 2024. Photograph: ATPImages/Getty Images Syria Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes Verdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people died William Christou in Beirut Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.40 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Syrian court has sentenced the country’s former president Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia for crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 14-year civil war, in which about half a million people died. The two men fled to Moscow after being ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the dictatorial regime in just 11 days . The former president and his brother, who commanded the feared fourth division and was considered the regime’s top security official, oversaw a brutal crackdown in which government forces killed, arrested and tortured indiscriminately to crush protests that started in 2011. The court said Bashar al-Assad had been sentenced to death for crimes of “premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children” as well as “torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity”. View image in fullscreen Syrians celebrate the ruling outside the palace of justice in Damascus. Photograph: Bakr Alkasem/AFP/Getty Images It said it would pursue international legal avenues to try to prosecute the two men, but Russian officials have previously declined requests to extradite its former Syrian allies. The court also sentenced Atef Najib, Assad’s cousin and the former head of political security in Daraa, to death. Najib was responsible for the torture of a group of 15 young boys who had graffitied anti-Assad slogans on a wall in 2011 – an event that kicked off mass protests in the southern Syrian province, which then spread to the rest of the country. Najib’s trial was highly publicised, with pictures of him listening to proceedings while dressed in a prison uniform and held in a cage in court. The Syrian government has presented his trial as a landmark case in its pursuit of transitional justice, something experts say is key to healing divisions in the country. View image in fullscreen Atef Najib on trial in Damascus. Photograph: Mohammed Al Rifai/EPA Syria has experienced explosions of violence in the post-Assad era. About 1,500 mostly Alawite civilians were killed in a wave of retaliatory killings in March 2025 after militants loyal to al-Assad attacked security forces. Al-Assad belonged to the Islamic Alawite sect – a minority group in Syria – and enjoyed strong support in the group’s coastal heartland during his rule. In July 2025, more than 1,700 people were killed in massacres in the Druze-majority province of Suweida when local fighting evolved into sectarian killings. Low-level violence has continued in northern Syria until the present day, particularly targeting Alawite civilians. Syrian authorities have taken steps towards transitional justice, establishing committees and arresting Assad-era officials, in an effort to end intercommunal violence. Al-Assad became president in 2000 at the age of 34, inheriting power from his father, Hafez. He had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and was not initially supposed to be president, but became the heir after his brother, Basil, died in a car accident. Though styled as a young reformer who was supposed to allow some liberalisation in Syrian politics and its economy, his legacy was largely defined by his brutal response to the country’s revolution. Under his rule, Syria’s fearsome security apparatus was given a free hand to arrest, torture and kill civilians on an industrial scale. https://telex.hu/transtelex/2026/08/16/o.text: Menü Kereső Feltehetően orosz drónt lőtt le a spanyol légierő Romániában, Bukarest erősebb NATO-légvédelmet kér Transtelex Vig Emese (Transtelex) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A NATO szerint minden bizonnyal orosz gyártmányú volt a drón , ami Moldovából repült át, és a spanyol légierő F–18-asai lőttek rá éles rakétát Galac megye felett. Martin O’Donnell amerikai ezredes, az észak-atlanti szövetség műveleti parancsnokságának szóvivője megerősítette: a részleteket még elemzik a szakértők, de az első adatok egyértelműen orosz eszközre utalnak. A NATO Légi Parancsnoksága (AIRCOM) az X-en közzétett beszámolójában részletezte a bevetést: a riasztott két spanyol F–18-as akcióját a spanyolországi Torrejónban működő Egyesített Légi Hadműveleti Központból koordinálták. A szövetség jelezte, a járőrszolgálatot éles légvédelmi készenlétre cserélték, ami lehetővé teszi, hogy ne csak kísérjék a határsértőket, hanem szükség esetén azonnal meg is semmisítsék őket. A most bevetett vadászgépek egy jóval nagyobb spanyol kontingenshez tartoznak, amely augusztus elején érkezett a Mihail Kogălniceanu bázisra: a spanyol légierő mintegy kétszáz fős legénységgel, hét F–18-assal, három NH–90-es drónelhárító helikopterrel és egy A400M légi utántöltő repülőgéppel települt Romániába egy négy hónapos rotációs misszióra. A légtérvédelmi akció után Oana Țoiu külügyminiszter telefonon egyeztetett spanyol kollégájával, José Manuel Albaresszel , és megköszönte a spanyol katonák gyors beavatkozását. Albares azonnal válaszolt, hogy a szövetségesek biztonsága közös ügy, Madrid ezért is küldte el azonnal a kért gépeket Romániába, és továbbra is kész megvédeni a román határt. A spanyol védelmi minisztérium közben az X-en dicsérte a saját katonáit, kiemelve, hogy a pilóták profi munkát végeztek az európai légtér védelmében. A román külügyminiszter a többi NATO-tagállamot is értesítette a történtekről, hozzátéve, hogy a mostani eset után Bukarest hivatalosan is kérni fogja a térség légvédelmének további erősítését. A vasárnapi akció során a járőröző két spanyol vadászgép hajnali 4:44-kor ért a Moldovai Köztársaság felől belépő légi célponthoz, majd 5:01-kor kapott engedélyt a megsemmisítésére. Az elmúlt hetekben ugrásszerűen megszaporodtak a román légteret és partvidéket érintő háborús incidensek. A védelmi minisztérium adatai szerint mindössze 96 óra leforgása alatt több mint száz drónt észleltek a radarok a román határ közelében, miközben az orosz erők az ukrajnai dunai kikötőket támadták. A Fekete-tenger hullámai Costinești, Saturn és Olimp strandjaira sodortak ki katonai dróndarabokat , emiatt a partszakaszt lezárták, és a nyaralókat eltiltották a fürdőzéstől. A vasárnapi lelövés már a negyedik olyan eset idén, amikor vadászgépek semmisítenek meg behatoló drónt Románia felett: július végén három egymást követő napon a román légierő F–16-osai lőttek le harci eszközöket Buzău megye, a Duna-delta és Sulina térségében. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-diplo.text: BIRMINGHAM, England — European diplomats are quietly courting Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, as the party gathers for its annual conference this week — with several EU countries sending representatives for the first time. Germany, Italy and Spain are among the nations dispatching officials to the party’s conference in Birmingham, as capitals begin to grapple with the prospect of Farage’s party entering government. “There are more [diplomats] attending this year, probably, because embassies realize more and more Reform UK is a political party that we have to take seriously, and it’s good to have contacts across political parties,” one EU diplomat, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic engagement, told POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement “This is how we get a better understanding of the policies and ambitions [of Reform], and also our way to share our views, [for example] on the importance of European cooperation,” the diplomat added. Farage’s party has seen a decline in public support over the course of 2026, but is still neck-and-neck in the polls with the governing Labour party, which is enjoying a polling bounce after the appointment of Andy Burnham as prime minister in July. Unwinding the reset A Farage government would pose challenges for the European Union. Reform has pledged to unwind the “reset” deals that the Labour government is negotiating with Brussels — and renegotiate the post-Brexit trade deal. It also wants to revisit the U.K.’s migrant returns deal with France, while removing EU settled status for welfare claimants and student loans for foreign nationals. Tensions between the EU and Reform have remained high over the last year, with the bloc considering a so-called “Farage clause” designed to protect the reset from being rolled back by a future government. Farage, however, has already warned he would “not honour any clause.” Berlin, Rome and Madrid aren’t the only capitals sending delegates in an effort to improve ties with the party. Advertisement Advertisement Representatives from Denmark, Norway, Finland, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Ireland, the Netherlands, Poland, and Romania are also expected to descend on Birmingham’s National Exhibition Centre for this week’s conference, according to multiple people familiar with embassy plans. Officials attending this year are largely political affairs officers and other diplomats, rather than the ambassadors themselves — a signal that European capitals are looking to establish contact with Reform without elevating the engagement to the highest diplomatic level. “As an embassy, it’s our responsibility to monitor all domestic developments in the host country,” a second EU diplomat said. “For that reason, we aim to follow as many party conferences as possible, either in person or through other means.” Staying away However, one notable European nation appears to be keeping its distance. France will not be sending representatives to this year’s conference, two EU diplomats told POLITICO — as Reform UK invites Jordan Bardella, president of France’s far-right National Rally, to address Farage’s supporters on Friday. The French embassy did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication. Advertisement Advertisement French President Emmanuel Macron visited Downing Street on Thursday morning for his first bilateral meeting with British prime minister Andy Burnham, before heading to the British Museum to see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition, which has returned to England from France for the first time in more than 900 years. Reform’s conference is expected to draw around 2,000 more attendees than last year, according to internal figures. Reform declined to comment on the increased embassy engagement. Clea Caulcutt contributed to this report.

The directive to prioritize immigrant visas at the U.S. missions in Poland and Hungary came from the White House, two of the sources said. While it was not immediately clear why the U.S. singled out the two countries for special attention, Trump and his senior aides have cultivated far-right allies in both places. He publicly endorsed former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who was defeated at the polls in April, and Poland's nationalist President Karol Nawrocki, whose election has put him at odds with the centrist government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. In May, Reuters reported that U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau instructed senior State Department officials to facilitate a U.S. visa for a fugitive former Polish cabinet minister who had taken refuge from corruption charges in Hungary. The White House referred a request for comment to the State Department. A State Department spokesperson did not comment on why it resumed immigrant visa processing for Hungary and Poland. The Hungarian Foreign Ministry and Prime Minister's Office, as well as the Polish Foreign Ministry, and prime minister’s and president’s offices did not immediately respond to requests for comment. TRUMP TARGETS BOTH ILLEGAL AND LEGAL MIGRATION Trump has long campaigned on stopping illegal immigration, but his second term has been defined in equal measure by his expansive efforts to curb legal migration. The U.S. has imposed travel bans on dozens of countries, introduced expensive new fees for certain work visas and mandated that all applicants undergo a vetting of their social media history. In January, the State Department said it was temporarily suspending the processing of immigrant visas — which allow people to move permanently to the United States — in 75 countries where applicants were "at a high risk for becoming a public charge." After a federal judge ruled against the visa ban, the State Department paused immigrant visa interviews at all of its global missions while rolling out a new training program. The State Department spokesperson, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said appointments were being adjusted to accommodate the new training. "Whenever there are updated instructions for visa applicants or changes to visa interview appointments, embassies and consulates communicate this information directly to visa applicants," they wrote. GLOBAL IMPACT U.S. consulates and embassies traditionally conduct hundreds of thousands of immigrant visa interviews every year, most of them with relatives of U.S. citizens or permanent residents. In 2024, the last year of Joe Biden's Democratic presidency, the U.S. issued some 600,000 immigrant visas. The State Department’s January edict was its most far-reaching attempt to rein in legal migration. The visa suspension affected applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil, Colombia, and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; and South Asian countries Pakistan and Bangladesh. On August 21, however, U.S. District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas struck down the policy as "patently unlawful." In the days that followed, the State Department called missions around the world and told them to cancel immigrant visa appointments, according to two people with knowledge of the situation. The State Department acknowledged the global pause in a public statement on August 25, saying it would remain in place until staffers received new training in how to assess whether visa applicants could support themselves in the United States without relying on public benefits. The U.S. government said in a court filing that interviews were temporarily rescheduled through August 31. But the suspension could remain in place for months due to the structure of the new training program. Missions need to self-train based on materials sent from Washington; a consular officer then needs to visit each post to certify that the training has been completed, a person familiar with the matter said. On a Reddit thread, people from around the world, including Peru, the United Kingdom and India, posted about canceled visa appointments through September. https://www.dw.com/en/famine-threatens-t.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5N4at The town of Oleshky in the Cherson region has been cut off from food deliveries since May Image: Anna Voitenko/REUTERS Advertisement A man sends a photo of "Oleshky borsch," a vegetable soup he has made from leftovers. To make the soup more filling, he says he has added millet and two eggs. "Today, we have a delicacy in our borsch. My mother traded 2.5 kilograms (5.5 pounds) of sugar for 10 eggs," he tells the recipient of the photo, Tetiana Hasanenko, the head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, which is based in territory controlled by Kyiv. "There's no cabbage in it, but there is asparagus," he adds. Hasanenko says she's used to getting such messages. "I receive reports like this every day," Hasanenko told DW. "People want to be given some kind of hope, but there is no hope." She said food was last delivered to the town at the end of May. "The situation is critical ," she said, warning that "you can't just call this starvation — it's a famine ." Oleshky is located in Ukraine's southern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River. The city has been occupied since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. In June 2023, the town was almost completely flooded after a blast at the Kakhovka Power Plant and the breach of the Kakhovka Dam. Hasanenko said the situation worsened last winter. She said there were about 6,000 people left in the area, including 180 children. They have already become accustomed to living without electricity and gas and have to fetch water from wells. Now, they have to prepare for another harsh winter. The destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in southern Ukraine has flooded Oleshky and left many basements full of food inaccessible for months Image: AP Photo/picture alliance 'One kilo of zucchini for 1,000 rubles' "To be honest, I haven't eaten anything yet," resident Halyna (whose name has been changed for security reasons) told DW by phone at around lunchtime. "My best option for today is a flatbread made of water and flour, as there's still some left. I spread apple sauce on it and make myself some tea without sugar. That's about it." People only go out between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m., she explained, adding that they tended to gather in the market square to hear the latest news and would trade or sell food from their supplies or gardens. "Today, there were a few zucchinis for 1,000 rubles (€10 or $11.4) per kilo," she said, adding that someone had sold a large sack of flour for 200,000 rubles. She speculated that he was probably going to try to leave Oleshky, which is why the price was so high. Minibuses used to run from Oleshky to Skadovsk about an hour south and then to Crimea or Russia. They also transported food to Oleshky for sale. After they were attacked by drones, two ambulances were deployed instead. "But for the past month and a half, none of the ambulances have been running, because one of the drivers was killed on a trip," Halyna reported. She explained that people are now stocking up on food in the village of Radensk, located 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) to the south. People walk there or ride their bikes. Anyone who wants to be evacuated must reach the village of Tarasivka, which is another 20 kilometers away. From there, you can get to Skadovsk by minibus or by hitchhiking. However, the route is heavily mined. "You set out and could die along the way," Halyna said, adding that two women who were trying to get food died that way. According to Halyna, scores of people in Oleshky have been injured by mines and explosive devices. But they can't count on medical help. "If your leg is blown off, you're as good as dead. There's a surgeon at the hospital, but no anesthesiologist and no medicine," she said. Conditions are also deteriorating for inpatients. "Last winter, they still got some soup and two pieces of baked dough," she said, adding that now there's one and a half spoonfuls of semolina porridge cooked in water and cold tea. Moreover, evacuating from Oleshky is difficult not only because of the danger of landmines. Many residents have neither a Russian nor a Ukrainian passport. In addition, people lack cash. Ukrainian authorities say that Russia has been slow in creating a humanitarian evacuation corridor for the trapped civilians Image: Metin Aktas/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance Moscow lacks evacuation willingness "There is only one solution: A 'green corridor' must be established and the people evacuated. The occupying authorities must move the people deeper into the temporarily occupied territory," says Tetiana Hasanenko of the Ukrainian military administration. Talks about an evacuation from Oleshky have been ongoing since last spring. At that time, at the initiative of the Ukrainian parliamentary human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, city officials compiled a list of residents who wish to leave the municipality of Oleshky. "358 people need to be evacuated urgently," he wrote on social media. "These are only the ones we've heard about," he emphasized, noting that the town of Oleshky currently has more than 6,000 residents. "These people must be rescued because the town has become a death trap," the ombudsman said. According to him, preliminary agreements had been reached between Kyiv and Moscow . The Ukrainian military was to ensure a ceasefire, and the International Committee of the Red Cross was to assist with the evacuation. But Russia "has not reaffirmed its willingness" to carry out the evacuation "for quite some time," Lubinets said. Meanwhile, the residents of Oleshky are desperate, says Tetiana Hasanenko. "They had hoped that the evacuation would begin at any moment. But what now? I can't give them any hope at all," she laments. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/06/latv.text: Latvian filmmaker Nikolay Shestak has won the $450,000 (€401,000) Grand Prix at the first Astana AI Film Festival in Kazakhstan for his film The First Honest Day, created using artificial intelligence.The First Honest Day explores how people's actions shape who they become, with bad deeds making its characters physically uglier and good deeds changing them for the better.Shestak, who started directing around four years ago and began making films with AI two years ago, said he did not expect to win."Honestly, I didn't expect to win. There were so many incredible works and different genres here that I'm curious myself why the jury chose my film," he said.He plans to invest the prize money in making new films and developing his projects.Second place in the main competition went to Indian filmmaker Abhik Banerjee for SITARA, earning him $200,000 (€178,000), while Spain's Ernest Desumbila received $100,000 (€89,000) for Looking For Perseida in third place.Another $250,000 (€223,000) was distributed across five categories in the open competition, with each winner receiving $50,000 (€44,000).Kazakh filmmaker Myrzakhan Zhumakhan won Best Character for his comedy It Was Just a Joke. China's 2xLabs won Best Story for The Last Span, while Italian filmmaker Jacopo Zanetti received Best Visual for What's the Job?. Another Italian filmmaker, Jacopo Reale, won Best Direction for The Fracture, and US filmmaker Zachary London took Best Concept for Pomegranate.The films were judged not only on how AI tools were used but also on their artistic vision, storytelling and overall coherence, as well as how organically the technology was integrated into the creative concept.The international jury included Audrey Azoulay, former Director-General of UNESCO and former French Culture Minister, Ping Ma of China Film Group, Wang Hao of Beijing Film Academy, entrepreneur and investor Balaji Srinivasan, and BytePlus executive Long Li.This year's competition attracted more than 8,000 submissions from 125 countries, with 25 films selected for the final programme. The projects span 19 genres and were created using more than 80 generative AI models.A festival drawing thousands of AI filmmakersThe festival had a total fund of $2 million (€1.8mn). Half of it, provided by the Freedom Shapagat Corporate Foundation under Freedom Holding Corp., was allocated to prize money.Another half was set aside as investment capital for promising AI teams and the development of production in Kazakhstan.Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who opened the festival, highlighted how artificial intelligence is changing the industry."Filmmakers and production crews no longer need to knock on the doors of production companies or look for sponsors. The barrier to entry has become significantly lower," he said.At the same time, Tokayev said AI would not replace the creative role of filmmakers, but could become "an indispensable tool for everyone who has devoted their life to creativity."He also said the festival was timely for Kazakhstan, pointing to the country's young population."Kazakhstan is a country of young people. The average age of our population is 33. I consider Kazakh youth educated, open to new ideas, intelligent and thoughtful," Tokayev said.For AAIFF co-founder and creative director Aizat Kussainov, the rapid pace of development in artificial intelligence was one of the main reasons to launch the festival."The driving force of this festival was FOMO. We had a fear of missing the opportunity because the technology is moving very fast," Kussainov said."But no one had actually created a festival like this, and we wanted to be the first in the world — and we did it. We had the biggest AI film festival in the world."Kussainov said the ambition goes beyond staging the festival itself and is also about bringing international creators to Kazakhstan."The main goal actually was not the festival. It was bringing the whole creative community here to Astana and making them see how our country is developing. We want them to move here and start creating their new movies from here," he said.The competition films were also screened for the public in cinemas in Astana, allowing audiences to see the films selected for the festival and how artificial intelligence is being used in filmmaking.

https://praguemonitor.com/pm/europe-worl.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Non-EU visitors without a residence permit or long-stay visa may stay in the Schengen area for up to 90 days in any rolling 180-day period. The 180 days are not a fixed calendar block: on any day you check, you look back over the 180 days ending on that day and count your days of stay. Stays on a Czech long-stay visa or residence permit do not count towards the 90 days, and EU citizens are not subject to the rule. On this page 9 sections What the rule says Five myths about the count How the window works A worked example What does not count Tools and consequences Keep your own record Staying in Czechia longer Your own count Many visitors count the rule wrongly. They picture "90 days in, 90 days out", like a quarterly cycle. The Schengen rule is a rolling window, and the count moves on every day, not every three months. The classic mistake is to assume that a short trip home resets the clock. It does not, and a traveller who overstays by a few days can end up with a fine, an entry ban or trouble at the next visa application. The rule in three numbers days you may spend in the Schengen area 90 days in the rolling window used for the count 180 days you look back from the day being checked; with that day itself they make the 180 179 Source: Schengen Borders Code; European Commission (as of 2026; check the official source) What the rule says A non-EU national who may enter the Schengen area without a visa, or with a short-stay visa, may stay for a maximum of 90 days in any period of 180 days. The limit applies to the area as a whole, not country by country. Ninety days in Czechia followed by 90 in Austria is not allowed, because the days are added up across the area. The rule comes from the Schengen Borders Code and applies to everyone subject to it. The Ministry of the Interior explains how it works for short stays in Czechia. There are exceptions, covered below. For the area itself, see Schengen area and Czechia . Five myths about the count The first myth is the reset. People assume that after a trip home the clock starts again. It does not: the window is rolling, so what matters on any given day is the total of your days in the previous 180. The second is that days in different countries are separate. They are not; the 90 days are pooled across the whole area. The third is that the day of arrival does not count. It does, as does the day of departure, even if you were there for a few hours. The fourth is that the window starts on a fixed calendar date. It does not; there is no fixed starting point, only the moving period that ends on the day being checked. The fifth is that nobody will notice a small overstay. Officers read entry and exit stamps and can count the days, and the Entry/Exit System is designed to make that count automatic. How the window works On any given day, look back 179 days from that day. With the day itself, that makes a 180-day window. Count each day in the window on which you were physically in the Schengen area. If the total is 90 or fewer, you are within the rule that day. If it is above 90, you are overstaying. Three conventions matter. The day of entry and the day of exit both count as full days, even if you were there for a few hours. Every day counts whether you spent it in one Schengen state or moved between several. And the window moves forward with each new day, so old days drop out at the back as new ones are added at the front. How to count your days Pick the day you want to check Usually today, or the planned day of your next exit. Go back 179 days That day and the 179 before it form the 180-day window. List every day you were in the area Entry and exit days both count in full. Add them up 90 or fewer: you are within the rule on that day. More than 90: you are overstaying. Repeat for the day you plan to leave The window moves, so the answer changes daily. A worked example This is an illustration, not an official calculation. Suppose a traveller spends 80 days in the Schengen area, leaves for 30 days and then returns. On the day of return, the 180-day window reaches back about six months. It still contains all 80 days of the first stay, because only 110 days have passed since that stay began. The traveller has used 80 of the 90 days and has 10 left. On the tenth day of the second stay the total in the window is 90. On the eleventh it would be 91, and the traveller is overstaying. The days of the first stay would not begin to drop out of the window until roughly 70 days after the return, long after the limit has been hit. The reverse also holds. A traveller who stays away long enough sees earlier days leave the window, and the allowance recovers day by day. It is fully back only when all earlier days have left the window, and a shorter gap restores only part of it. Who is subject to the 90/180 rule? Traveller Subject to the rule? Visa-free visitor from outside the EU Yes Holder of a short-stay Schengen visa Yes Holder of a Czech long-term permit, on a trip to another Schengen state Yes, for the short stay there Holder of a Czech long-stay visa or permit, in Czechia No, they are staying under the permit EU, EEA or Swiss citizen No General outline; exceptions and bilateral agreements exist. Check the Ministry of the Interior. Not legal advice This describes the general rule. If your case involves a change of permit or a gap between documents, ask the Ministry of the Interior or a qualified immigration lawyer. What does not count Time spent in the Schengen area on a national long-stay visa or a residence permit issued by a Schengen state does not count towards the 90 days. A long-term Czech residence permit, for example, lets you live in Czechia for the permit's period. Holders of such permits can also travel in the rest of the area for short stays of up to 90 days in any 180, subject to the rules, and days spent in other Schengen states count in the same way for them. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens are not subject to the rule, and nor are family members of EU citizens exercising free movement rights, under the conditions in EU law. A few nationalities have bilateral agreements with particular Schengen states that allow longer stays (as of 2026; check the Ministry of the Interior). Tools and consequences The European Commission offers an online short-stay calculator that shows how many days you have left. Use it, and keep your travel history, such as boarding passes and tickets. The EU is also introducing a digital Entry/Exit System that records entries and exits at the external border, which will make the count visible to border officers; check the official EU source for its status. Overstaying can lead to fines, a removal order and an entry ban, and it can affect later visa and permit applications. If your case is complicated, because of a change of permit or a gap between documents, ask the Ministry of the Interior or a qualified immigration lawyer. This article describes the general rule and is not legal advice. Keep your own record The surest protection is a record you keep yourself. Save boarding passes, train tickets and accommodation bookings, and write the dates of each entry and exit in a single list as you go. A stamp can be faint or missing, an airline's email can disappear and an officer can ask you to account for a trip from last year. If the dates in your list agree with the stamps in your passport, a check takes minutes. If they do not, you will have a hard conversation about which version is right. Frequent travellers who split their time between Czechia and neighbouring countries are the group who most often fall foul of the rule, because their trips are short and their sense of the count is vague. For them the calculator is not a one-off but a habit: run it before booking a trip, not after. Staying in Czechia longer To live, study or work in Czechia for longer than a short stay, you need a long-stay visa or a residence permit. These are applied for through the Ministry of the Interior's procedures and, in most cases, at a Czech embassy abroad. They are a different route from the 90/180 rule, so check the procedure for your nationality and purpose before you travel. Your own count Write down your entry and exit dates for the last 180 days, then run them through the Commission's short-stay calculator to see your remaining allowance before you book your next trip. Keep the result with your travel records. Frequently asked questions Does a day trip count as a day? Yes. The day of entry and the day of exit each count in full, however short the visit. Do I get a fresh 90 days after 90 days outside? Not as a block. Days leave the window one by one, so the allowance recovers gradually unless you stay away long enough for all earlier days to drop out. Is the limit per country? No. It applies to the whole Schengen area, so days in Czechia, Austria and Germany are added together. Where can I check my count? The European Commission's online short-stay calculator. https://www.dw.com/en/senegal-youth-olym.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PRIa Prefer DW on Google The Summer Youth Olympics in Dakar was held from October 31 to November 13 Image: Sylvain Cherkaoui/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement The Senegal Summer Youth Olympics in Dakar ended Friday after two weeks of games on a high note. It's the first time an African country has hosted an Olympic event, and African nations also brought home a record haul of medals. The Games were met with enthusiasm, with Dakar's streets and beaches filled with sports fans. Nearly 2,700 young athletes took part in the games, which featured 153 medal events across 25 sports. IOC president on Senegal games: 'Expectations have been exceeded' "There is a beautiful African proverb, 'It take a village to raise a child.' And if these Youth Olympic Games have shown us anything it is what can happen when an entire country comes together for its young people," International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said in a thank-you ceremony on Friday. Coventry praised the Senegalese people for hosting the games: "You have shown the world what Senegal and Africa are capable of, and when people come together behind a shared dream, how strong that can make us. You have every reason to be so proud." She said earlier in the week that "expectations have been exceeded" when it came to Senegal hosting the games and that it shows what African nations are capable of in the future. Which countries took home the most medals? China took home the most gold medals at 18. Japan took home 11 gold medals, whereas Russia received eight. It was the first time Russian athletes took part in an Olympic event under their own national flag since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022 . Egypt won six gold medals, and Ethiopia and Senegal each earned five. Female wrestler Elisabeth Diatta, who is 16 years old, took home Senegal's first gold medal Image: Kadir Caliskan/United World Wrestling/picture alliance It was the first time Senegal had ever won an Olympic gold, with 136 Senegalese athletes participating in the games. The next Summer Youth Olympics will take place in 2030, with Chile, Paraguay and Thailand having confirmed their bids to host the games.
